prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose, rooted in poetry, that builds memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation into large-scale imaginative architectures.

statement.case_for: I keep B014 first after rereading the opening files. The case rests on distinctiveness of voice and on the scale and coherence of the imaginative project. The longlist text and public knowledge place Blinding and Solenoid in a single world in which memory, the body, dream and cosmology are worked through the same dense syntax. Poetry is the base of that prose, so the citation can cover a recognisable whole, not one title. The oeuvre has a long arc from poetry to the major prose cycles, which speaks to sustained quality. Attribution is unambiguous and the citation scope is clean. Among the shortlisted writers, he offers the strongest combination of formal ambition, imaginative depth and a body of work that can be cited as a whole. I am not counting the convergence of first-place rankings as merit. My preference rests on the literary reasons above, which I have re-examined against colleagues' reservations.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one Ellen Mattson also names: length and elaboration may shade into repetition in some volumes, and the density of the Romanian sentence reaches us only through translators of varying quality. I have not independently verified the texts, and my view of the poetry and early work is thinner than my view of the major novels. If the committee's translated reading cannot establish that the metaphysical architecture sustains itself beyond the best-known novels, the case for the whole oeuvre is weaker than it first appears. A second, related reservation is that such a visionary and inward project may be more impressive in outline than in sentence-level execution, which translation hides from us.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis second on formal and linguistic achievement in Arabic, but warns that translation loses much of the prosodic and intertextual work. He also says controversy around the writer's statements is not literary evidence. He places Can Xue eighth because the philosophical depth is harder to assess from translation.
responses.response: I agree that Adonis's claim lies in Arabic diction and prosody, which we can mostly assess only through reputation and secondary accounts. That is why I keep him as an alternative and not my first choice. I also agree that his politics and essays cannot substitute for the poetry, so any citation should be confined to the renewal of Arabic poetic language. I do not think the translation problem is a reason to rank Can Xue as low as eighth. The same limitation applies to Adonis and to Cărtărescu, and I see no principled basis for applying it unevenly. I would rather treat it as a shared uncertainty. Her case needs more evidence on development across the corpus before I would move her above him.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Adonis seventh. He finds it hard to separate the essays and cultural criticism from the poetry when assessing literary achievement, and he notes that public discussion of the writer is entangled with politics. He ranks Michon fourth for compression and style but worries about the small corpus.
responses.response: That difficulty is real and it qualifies my own second-place ranking. His editorial and critical influence on Arabic poetry is part of the story, but the will asks us to weigh literary work, and the citation should rest on the poems. Where I differ is that I would not read the entanglement with politics as lowering the poetic claim. It only says we must not count it. On Michon, I share the concern about breadth and rank him seventh for the same reason. A very small, finely made corpus may deserve recognition, but I cannot show from the supplied material that the oeuvre has the range to carry a prize for the whole body of work.

responses.point: Sward ranks Can Xue second as a radically original voice with formal rigour that does not depend on political symbolism. She also admits that the deliberately repetitive and oblique method makes it hard to judge variation and development, and that the translated proportion of the oeuvre is uncertain.
responses.response: That is a fair and candid account, and it moves me to take Can Xue's claim more seriously than my fourth-place ranking suggested. Her unmistakable method is a genuine strength. My hesitation is the one Sward names: if the method is deliberately uniform, then depth across decades is hard to show from a partial translated corpus, and I would need that evidence before preferring her to Cărtărescu. Her work and his also differ in architecture. His builds cumulatively across large forms, while hers works through repeated estrangement in shorter pieces, so the unity of the oeuvre is harder to state in a citation. For that reason I keep her as my second alternative and not my preferred candidate, but I do not think the committee should dismiss her.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for a voice recognisable nowhere else and a coherent whole-career achievement. She flags the risk that length and elaboration become repetition in some volumes, and that the effect depends on Romanian sentence rhythm that she can only judge in translation.
responses.response: Her reservation is my own strongest one, and I do not think it can be settled from the material before us. I would not overweight it, though, because the opening files give no concrete evidence that the repetition is more than a risk of scale. I would ask colleagues who know the translated novels and poetry well to say which volumes they consider weakest, so that the citation does not claim more than the corpus supports. If the committee's reading shows the late work only repeating the earlier motifs, I would revisit my ranking. At present the evidence points to extension and not repetition.

uncertainties: Whether the metaphysical density and formal control of Cărtărescu's prose sustain themselves across the whole corpus, including poetry and early work, and not mainly in the best-known novels.

Translation quality for Romanian, Arabic and Chinese prose and poetry, where much of the claimed achievement lies in the sentence and prosody. I have not read the originals or independently verified the sources.
Corpus coverage in translation for Can Xue and Adonis is uncertain, and so is whether Can Xue's method deepens or repeats.
How far the essays and public commentary of Adonis should enter a citation focused on the poetry.
Whether a co-opted member's vote counts in committee is not documented in the supplied profile, so my simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I am co-opted as Permanent Secretary and my own work is non-fiction, which is context and not evidence of any preference for a candidate. The profile records no connection to any shortlisted writer.
